questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere outside Europe to an English-speaking country. Also, Toronto being a big city and UofT being a good university had a big impact on my decision.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The only downside to choosing Toronto is that it's an expensive city to live in. But with a little bit of savings four months is completely fine.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy for the most part. As long as you check your email and make the necessary 'university-profiles' you will be fine. Also, join the Facebook group created from UofT as soon as it's available for you - they also provide some information regarding the arrival here. If there's something you're uncertain about it also helps to ask other students from UCPH going to your university.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Not very much (some emails) - most of the information we got before arriving.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I stayed at Tartu College which I found throughout reading travel reports from from students being at UofT before me. However, a lot of students had problems with finding housing so it's important to start looking for it early.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: We're not allowed to live on campus at UofT as exchange students so it's important to start looking for housing early in the application process. I can really recommend living at Tartu College (very close to the city centre and UofT St. George campus and one of the cheapest options in the city - and you live with a lot of other exchange student which is a very good start to getting to know people in the city. Also, not a lot of places allow you to stay for only one semester - but Tartu does!). However, as I recall the application is already in April (before you have formally been accepted to UofT) so if you're somewhat sure to be accepted I would recommend to apply on the day they open for fall registration. Otherwise you're pretty sure not to get a room there.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: ^ I had a very good experience with housing but I know a lot of other students who had big issues with finding a place to stay.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was very easy. We looked at the different courses in the course catalogue and then we had to fill out a Google Forms. Also, I think we chose courses before "their own students" so you have a good chance of getting the courses that you want - and they have multiple rounds where you can apply and drop courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could write and email to the registration office. They were very helpful and responded fast.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted. (If this is relevant for you: At first I was told we weren't able to take laboratory courses, but then I wrote an email to the registration office and was allowed on the course anyway)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Check the course catalogue before registration opens so that you know kinda which courses you would like to take (they have a lot to choose from).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic levels wasn't very different from classes at UCPH but their courses are build around a very different structure than at home.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Their grade from the courses is not just based on one final exam (as we know it from Copenhagen) but it consists of various assignments, midterms, participation and quizzes in addition to the final exam (different from every course how many of these the grade is based on) so you have a little more work to do during the semester but each part is "less important" compared to the single exam we have at home. Also, most midterms and final exams are multiple choice!

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
CSC108: Introduction to Computer Programming
HMB300: Neurobiology of Behaviour
HMB310: Laboratory in Neuroscience
PCL475: Neuropsychopharmacology 1

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Introduction to Computer Programming: Gives a good introduction to programming in Python. Workload: Weekly quizzes and three assignments in addition to a midterm and a final exam.

Neurobiology of Behaviour: Probably the "easiest" course regarding the workload. Gave a very interesting view into different neurological and psychological diseases/disorders. Workload: Weekly quizzes (however with unlimited tries) and two assignments in addition to a midterm and a final exam (however both of these two were online).

HMB310: Laboratory in Neuroscience: Very nice course with a smaller class size - and a nice break from "normal" classes with being in the lab (we had both wet lab and dry lab experiments). However, a bigger workload: Four assignments (however could drop one of them), quizzes weekly/every other week and one in-class presentation. However, no midterm and the final exam was a presentation of our project we worked on in the lab (was before the actual 'exam period' which was nice!).

PCL475: Neuropsychopharmacology 1: Gave an introduction to different brain diseases and how we treat them - also with a more psychological aspect. You could feel that it was a pharmacology course given that they talked a lot about different drugs (both medications and 'abuse' drugs) and how we use/used them. However very little workload with only one assignment and one midterm and final exam. Interesting to see diseases from another aspect compared to what we usually learn about in our degree at home and learn more about the different drugs we use to treat these diseases.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Because Canada usually is not included in different packages for insurance and phone services it can get a little bit more expensive. I can recommend getting a travel insurance through IDA and phone service from CBB - however, these might be a problem if you're away for more than four months.

Another unexpected cost was that we had to pay to get our transcript (which is required to get your courses transferred to your degree at UCPH) - however it's not that expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries (and alcohol) and public transportation was way more expensive than I imagined. However, most things cost approximately the same as in Copenhagen.

Take away and coffee (Tim Hortons!!) can be way cheaper than at home.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't participate much in clubs but we had a lot of different options to choose from.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The gym was free for all students and they offered a lot of different workout classes which was very nice! They also had different cultural clubs you could join and offered different social activities for students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Participate in the introduction events hosted by the university as this will be a good chance to meet other exchange students. Also, going to different workout classes and events at Hart House. And frat parties!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of different things to do in and around Toronto. Here are some daytrips you can take: Visit Niagara Falls or rent a car (very nice if one in your group is 25 or older - then it's way cheaper!) and go to a lake or park around Toronto - for instance Algonquin National Park is very nice especially in fall with the different coloured leaves!! You can also rent a cabin or an AirBnb and stay for the weekend. In Toronto I would really recommend Toronto Islands (!!!) especially going there to see the sunset. Also, Distillery District (especially for their Christmas market!), Eaton centre, walk along the habour front, and just in general walk around in the very nice city. Also, for going out: Definitely check out 'Pizza, Wine, Disco'! Also, going to other places in Canada. I went with friends to Montreal and Vancouver - and especially Vancouver was really amazing!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy - not very different from Copenhagen/Denmark. However, the students at the university is a little younger and at little less social than we're used to from home.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to them in the lectures and say that you're an exchange student - they don't really have that very much so many people will be interested to hear about your experiences in Toronto and where you're from. Or go to frat parties.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They are less social/used to going out than we're used to - most bars/discos close at 2/3 and are kinda empty around 1.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The culture is not that different from at home but being in a bigger city is very nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Participate in all the events/parties you're offered in the beginning so that you already make some friends from start and try to get a room in at student residence/live with other students! Also, know that it will take a little time to fully adjust and being away from home will be difficult - but it will be harder to say goodbye at the end :))

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: In the beginning we were "offered" to buy tickets to welcome parties. However, most of these were very expensive and were either rescheduled or cancelled without us getting our money back. So I don't know if I would recommend buying these tickets. Most clubs/bars are free (at least for girls - and also guys for the most part as long as you get a free ticket and go there before midnight) - @uoftparties provides link/tickets to the free clubs/bars every week and is a great place to start).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Making friends from all over the world and just being 'on your own' in another country without having any responsibilities other than taking care of yourself. Also, it was very nice that we just need to pass our courses and not depend on getting good grades (as most people do at home) - I know some of my friends from other countries felt like they spend too much time studying instead of exploring the city because they needed the grades (UofT is a hard university when you need to get good grades!).

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to the life at start - but it will not take long :))

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go, go, go!! It's the most amazing experience and something you will always remember - with great friends and a lot of fantastic memories!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
